summary.text: For an arbitrary bound, choose a sufficiently large \(M\) and apply the assumed decomposition to \(n=(M+1)!/6\), obtaining primes \(p=6x-1\) and \(q=6(n-x)+1\) with \((M+1)!=p+q\). If the resulting Sophie Germain prime were below the bound, then \(p\mid(M+1)!\) and hence \(p\mid q\); similarly, if the resulting twin pair were below the bound, then \(q\mid(M+1)!\) and hence \(q\mid p\), but primality would force a divisor to be \(1\) or the other prime, impossible since both are nontrivial and \(p\equiv-1\), \(q\equiv1\pmod 6\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{p\in\mathbb N:p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
T=\{p\in\mathbb N:p\text{ is prime and }p+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)=A227923(n)\) is the sum, over all integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), of the indicator of the following condition. Writing \(y=n-x\), the four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are all prime. Thus, if \(a(n)>0\), at least one summand is nonzero, so there are integers \(x,y\ge 1\) with \(x+y=n\) such that all four displayed numbers are prime. For such a decomposition, \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime, because
\[
2(6x-1)+1=12x-1,
\]
and \(6y-1,6y+1\) form a twin-prime pair.

Assume throughout that
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\]
We prove separately that \(S\) and \(T\) are unbounded. Any unbounded subset of \(\mathbb N\) is infinite, so this will prove both desired infinitude statements.

We first record the factorial construction that will be used in both parts. If \(N'\ge 5\), put
\[
M=N'+1,
\qquad
n=\frac{M!}{6}.
\]
Since \(M\ge 6\), the integer \(6\) divides \(M!\), so \(n\) is an integer and
\[
6n=M!.
\]
Also \(M!\ge 6!=720\), whence
\[
n=\frac{M!}{6}\ge 120>1.
\]
The hypothesis therefore supplies a decomposition \(n=x+y\), with \(x,y\ge1\), for which
\[
q:=6x-1,\qquad 2q+1=12x-1,
\]
and
\[
p:=6y-1,\qquad r:=6y+1=p+2
\]
are all prime. In particular, \(q\in S\), \(p\in T\), and the relation \(x+y=n\) gives the crucial identity
\[
r+q=(6y+1)+(6x-1)=6(x+y)=6n=M!.
\tag{1}
\]

We now prove that the Sophie Germain primes are unbounded. Let an arbitrary bound \(N\in\mathbb N\) be given, and choose
\[
N'=\max\{5,N\}.
\]
Use the preceding construction to obtain \(x,y,q,p,r\). We claim that \(q>N\). Suppose instead that \(q\le N\). Then
\[
q\le N\le N'<N'+1=M.
\]
Moreover \(x\ge1\), so \(q=6x-1\ge5\), in particular \(q\ge1\). Every positive integer at most \(M\) divides \(M!\); hence
\[
q\mid M!.
\]
By (1), \(M!=r+q\). Since \(q\) divides both \(M!\) and \(q\), it follows that
\[
q\mid M!-q=r.
\]
The number \(r=6y+1\) is prime. A positive divisor of a prime is either \(1\) or the prime itself, so there are two cases:

1. \(q=1\). This is impossible because \(x\ge1\) gives \(q=6x-1\ge5\).

2. \(q=r\). This is also impossible: \(q=6x-1\) is congruent to \(-1\pmod 6\), whereas \(r=6y+1\) is congruent to \(1\pmod 6\). Equality would imply \(-1\equiv1\pmod6\), or equivalently that \(6\) divides \(2\), which is false.

Both cases are impossible. Therefore \(q>N\). Since \(q\in S\), for every \(N\) there is a Sophie Germain prime larger than \(N\). Thus \(S\) is unbounded and consequently infinite.

It remains to prove that the twin primes are unbounded. Again let \(N\in\mathbb N\) be arbitrary, but this time choose
\[
N'=\max\{5,N+2\}.
\]
Apply the same factorial construction and the positivity hypothesis, obtaining primes
\[
q=6x-1,
\qquad
p=6y-1,

aqquad
r=6y+1=p+2
\]
with the factorial identity \(r+q=M!\), where \(M=N'+1\). We claim that the lower twin prime \(p\) is greater than \(N\).

Suppose, to the contrary, that \(p\le N\). Then its upper twin partner satisfies
\[
r=p+2\le N+2\le N'<N'+1=M.
\]
Since \(y\ge1\), we have \(r=6y+1\ge7\), so \(r\) is positive. Hence, as a positive integer no larger than \(M\), it divides \(M!\):
\[
r\mid M!.
\]
Using (1), \(M!=r+q\). Because \(r\) divides both \(M!\) and \(r\), subtraction gives
\[
r\mid M!-r=q.
\]
Now \(q=6x-1\) is prime. Therefore its positive divisor \(r\) must be either \(1\) or \(q\). Again there are two cases:

1. \(r=1\). This is impossible because \(y\ge1\) gives \(r=6y+1\ge7\).

2. \(r=q\). This is impossible because \(r=6y+1\equiv1\pmod6\), while \(q=6x-1\equiv-1\pmod6\). As above, equality would force \(6\mid2\).

Thus the assumption \(p\le N\) is untenable, and so \(p>N\). Since \(p\in T\), every bound \(N\) is exceeded by the lower member of some twin-prime pair. Therefore \(T\) is unbounded and hence infinite.

We have proved that the assumed positivity of \(A227923(n)\) for every \(n>1\) implies both infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
